title: Area X review: Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
intro: These questions mix the nine Tasks of Area X: slow flight, the Task B demonstration, power-off, power-on and accelerated stalls, the cross-controlled, elevator trim and secondary stall demonstrations, and spins. Many join two of them in one lesson flight, such as slow flight into a power-on stall, a power-off stall that turns into an elevator trim stall on the climb-out, or a cross-controlled stall that starts to spin.

questions.q: Last week you flew the Task B demonstration with a commercial learner, holding the edge of the stall and calling the horn out loud. Today, in calm air, he flies slow flight at a speed where the horn chirps on and off, says 'horn acknowledged' each time, and holds altitude within 30 feet. How do you grade it, and what is the fix?
options: Satisfactory: the CFI ACS lets a momentary warning go unpenalized, and calling it out each time is exactly the recognition that its Appendix 3 note asks for in this Task
Satisfactory: the slow flight altitude tolerance is ±100 feet, the same as in Task B, so a 30-foot hold with the warning called out meets both standards
Not to the standard: slow flight is flown with no stall warning, so lower the nose slightly and add power until it stops; holding the warning on purpose belongs only to the briefed Task B stop
Not to the standard, but only because the horn must sound steadily, not chirp; AC 61-67C has the learner hold heading and altitude with the warning device on
questions.why: Slow flight is now flown at a speed where the airplane is controllable without activating the stall warning, and any warning is corrected promptly [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]; the ACS says the same: "without a stall warning" (AI.X.A.S4), with altitude ±50 feet (AI.X.A.S5). The AFH way to find that speed is to slow to the warning, lower the nose slightly, add power and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. In Task B the warning is held on purpose and acknowledged aloud at the edge (AI.X.B.S4d), with ±100 feet (AI.X.B.S1), which is why the habit must be briefed as belonging to that stop only; failure to respond to a stall warning is a listed slow flight error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The Appendix 3 note excuses a momentary warning caused by turbulence that is promptly corrected, not a calm-air warning left on. AC 61-67C's 'warning device activated' line is the older practice [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(2)]].

questions.q: Stabilized in slow flight at the target speed, your learner wants a 200-foot descent at that same airspeed. He lowers the nose and leaves the power alone. What do you teach?
options: That is right: pitch sets the flightpath, so lowering the nose gives the descent and the airspeed stays at the target without any power change
Raise the nose slightly instead and leave the power alone, because the extra AOA slows the sink and the added drag holds the airspeed at the target
Add a little power and lower the nose more, because below L/DMAX the added thrust holds the airspeed while the lower pitch gives the descent
Ease the power back and lower the nose just enough to hold the target airspeed; in slow flight power sets the path and pitch sets the speed
questions.why: Climbs and descents in slow flight are made by adjusting the power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Below L/DMAX small pitch changes make large changes in induced drag and airspeed, so pitch is the effective airspeed control and power the effective path control [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. For a descent at constant speed, the AFH energy rule is less throttle and pitch down just enough to hold the speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Lowering the nose with the power unchanged trades altitude for speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]], so the airspeed climbs past the +5/-0 knot tolerance (AI.X.A.S5). Adding power raises total energy, which is the climb rule [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Raising the nose below L/DMAX slows the airplane toward the warning, not a steady speed [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

questions.q: On a go-around from a balked landing with full flaps, your learner adds full power and pulls the nose up at once to climb out of ground effect, barely above the stall speed. The airplane will not climb and the horn sounds. Which slow flight idea explains it, and what is the way out?
options: Reversed command: on the back side of the power curve even full power may not give a climb; lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed, accepting a little altitude, then climb and raise the flaps in small increments
Speed stability above L/DMAX: hold the attitude and wait, because the airspeed comes back by itself once the airplane is out of ground effect and the induced drag falls away
Not enough lift: the throttle is already full, so raise the nose and trim further nose-up, since a higher AOA always gives more lift and therefore a better climb at any airspeed
Adverse yaw from the flaps: level the wings with rudder alone and hold the pitch, because the horn is reacting to the sideslip from the flaps and not to the angle of attack
questions.why: The PHAK's reversed command examples are exactly this: climbing out of ground effect too slowly can leave the airplane unable to climb even at full power, and the only recourse is to lower the pitch and accept some altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. The AFH go-around text says an airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed, the pilot should resist any impulse to pitch up when the airspeed is insufficient, and it may be right to lower the nose briefly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; climbing prematurely out of ground effect is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]], and the flaps come up in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The speed instability that keeps a slow airplane decaying applies below L/DMAX, not above it [[24:115|AFH 5-10]], so waiting does not fix it. In the AFH energy example, when the airplane is so slow that even full throttle leaves no surplus power, the only way out is to push forward, cut the AOA and the induced drag, and only then add power [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. More nose-up is the opposite of that.

questions.q: Building the Task B ground brief, your learner marks 'reversed command starts here' at best glide speed (L/DMAX) on the power-required curve. Where do the CFI ACS and the PHAK put that line?
options: At L/DMAX, as she drew it, because minimum drag and minimum power required always fall at the same airspeed, so best glide is where more power first becomes necessary
At the minimum power required speed, the curve's lowest point, which the PHAK calls maximum endurance; minimum drag (L/DMAX) is a different point
At the bottom of the green arc (VS1), because reversed command is defined by the stall speed marking, and every speed above VS1 is in the region of normal command
At design maneuvering speed (VA), the S4a stop, because above VA more speed needs more power and below VA less speed needs more power to hold the altitude
questions.why: The ACS names the minimum power required speed and "its role in differentiating the region of normal command and the region of reversed command" (AI.X.B.K3). The PHAK puts reversed command below the speed for maximum endurance, the lowest point on the power curve [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]], and says the minimum power and maximum endurance point is a different point from minimum drag [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]]. Best glide occurs at L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]], so it is not the line, even though the AFH slow flight text uses L/DMAX as a shorthand [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. VS1 and VA are airspeed limits, not points that divide the power curve.

questions.q: At the S4a stop of the clean Task B demonstration, your learner says, 'We are at VA, so nothing can break. I will move the rudder and ailerons fully together, then reverse them, to show how the airplane responds.' What do you tell him?
options: He is right: at or below VA no control input, in any number of axes or in any order, can overstress the airplane, so the demonstration is safe to fly
He is right today, because the airplane is light and VA gets higher as weight comes down, which allows more of the control travel to be used at once
He has the wrong speed: full control movement is limited by VNO, the top of the green arc, and below that line every combination of inputs is safe
He is wrong: VA covers one full input in one axis, not several at once or large reversals, which can overstress the airplane even below VA
questions.why: VA is the highest speed at which full control deflection or a gust can be imposed without structural damage, and it is lower, not higher, when the airplane is light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. It gives no structural protection against multiple full control inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. AC 61-67C adds that rapid, large alternating inputs can cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]. VNO is a different limit, the maximum structural cruising speed [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. At S4a the ACS asks you to hold VA or VO for today's weight (AI.X.B.S4a); fly smooth, single inputs.

questions.q: At the S5d stop, holding the edge of the stall with full flaps, your learner sees the altitude sag 40 feet and gives the yoke a quick tug to get it back. The buffet turns into a break. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: An accelerated stall from pulling too fast: at the edge any added AOA or load factor stalls at once; use small, smooth inputs, power for altitude, and reduce AOA first if it stalls
A power-off stall caused by the flaps: raise them to the takeoff setting before the S5d stop, because full flaps are only used for the acceleration in S5f, not at the edge
The right priority, badly timed: 40 feet was already past the ±100-foot tolerance for this Task, so a quick pull to win back the altitude had to come first, before power or anything else
A secondary stall, because the warning had been on too long: the fix is to trim nose-up before reaching the edge so the horn stays silent while the learner holds the stop
questions.why: S5d is the airspeed where any further increase in AOA or load factor, or reduction in power, would stall immediately (AI.X.B.S5d), so a tug there stalls the wing. 'Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on the controls' is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and abrupt or rough control movements in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Altitude at the edge is held with power, which is needed as the speed nears the target [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. If it stalls, the most important action is to reduce the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A 40-foot sag is inside ±100 feet (AI.X.B.S1), and S5d is flown with gear and flaps fully extended (AI.X.B.S5d), so neither tempting excuse holds.

questions.q: In a power-off straight-ahead stall, your learner holds the yoke full aft against the stop while the airplane sinks fast. He says, 'There is almost no buffet, so we have not stalled yet.' What do you teach?
options: It has stalled: in a power-off 1G stall the buffet is less noticeable, and the main cues may be the yoke full aft against the stop and a high descent rate
He is right: buffet is the one reliable stall cue, so he should keep the yoke full aft until the buffet builds up strongly, and only then recover from it
He is right until the airspeed reaches the bottom of the green arc, because the published stall speed is where the wing stalls in every condition
The nose is not high, so the wing cannot be stalled; a stall needs a nose-high attitude, and the sink comes only from the power being off
questions.why: In a power-off stall the cues (buffeting, shaking) are less noticeable than in a power-on stall, and in a power-off 1G stall the predominant cue may be the elevator control position (full up elevator against the stops) and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The most important action is then to reduce the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. It is possible to exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, attitude and power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], and vision is not a foolproof stall cue [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. The published 1G stall speed holds only in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], so the bottom of the green arc is not a trigger [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

questions.q: Flying a left turning power-off stall at 15° of bank from a heading of 090, your learner plans to vary the bank so the break comes exactly on 360, 'like rolling out on a heading'. What do you teach?
options: Good plan: the ±10° heading tolerance applies to the turning stall as well, so the break must come within 10° of a heading the learner chooses before the entry
Hold a constant, coordinated 15° bank and do not try to stall on a set heading; expect the break within about 90° of turn, as in a turn from base to final
Fly it wings level instead, because the CFI ACS keeps turning stalls for the power-on Task only and uses bank only in the cross-controlled demonstration
Let the bank steepen as the speed decays, because more bank brings the stall sooner and keeps the turn inside 90°, the most heading change the ACS permits
questions.why: The AFH says no attempt should be made to stall or recover on a predetermined heading, but to simulate the base-to-final turn the stall normally should come within a heading change of about 90°; the turn continues at a constant bank, coordinated, until the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Failure to maintain a constant bank in turning stalls is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The ACS ±10° applies to the heading in straight flight; in turning flight the standard is the specified bank, not to exceed 20°, ±5° (AI.X.C.S6). A steepening bank in a skid can go to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

questions.q: You finish slow flight with a private learner at 50 knots, full flaps, holding 3,500 feet. Next is a straight-ahead power-on stall, and she says, 'We're already slow and nose-high, so I'll leave the flaps down, go to full power right here and pull.' What do you teach?
options: Set the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration, slow to lift-off speed, then set no less than 65 percent power and raise the nose smoothly
Good plan: slow flight is the ideal entry, because the AFH adds full power at the slowest speed the pilot can hold so that the stall comes with the least altitude lost
Keep the flaps down but set only 50 percent power, because the CFI ACS caps power-on stalls at half power to hold the pitch below 30° in every training airplane
Accelerate to cruise first, then pull up briskly at full power, because a power-on stall has to start from cruise speed to show the left-turning forces at their strongest
questions.why: Power-on stalls are flown in the takeoff configuration, and also clean; the pilot slows to normal lift-off speed and only then sets takeoff or climb power, to avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The ACS asks for the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration as the evaluator specifies (AI.X.D.S3) and no less than 65 percent power (AI.X.D.S4); full flaps is the landing configuration. 65 percent is a floor, not a cap: Appendix 3 lets some high-performance airplanes use less only to keep the pitch at or below 30°. Then the nose comes up smoothly, since pulling too fast on a power-on entry is the accelerated stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

questions.q: In slow flight at low power your learner held the ball centered with a modest push on the right pedal. Now, in a takeoff-configuration power-on stall at full power, the ball drifts right and the nose slides left as the nose comes up. He says, 'I'm holding the same right rudder as in slow flight.' What do you tell him?
options: That is enough: once climb power is set the left-turning forces stay constant, so a ball slightly right is normal and the stall recovery will center it again
Use left aileron instead of more rudder, because P-factor is a rolling force, and the ailerons are the control that balances it at high power and low airspeed
Reduce the power below 65 percent so the slow flight rudder is enough, because the CFI ACS lets the instructor choose any power that keeps the ball centered
Add right rudder progressively as the speed decays, all the way to the stall: at full power and high AOA the slipstream and P-factor yaw grow
questions.why: In the power-on stall entry, as the airspeed decreases the pilot moves the elevator progressively back while adding right rudder, all the way to the full stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The AFH slow flight text says the same thing in general: the closer to the stall and the higher the power, the more right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. The PHAK ties the corkscrew slipstream to high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in power-on stall approaches [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]], and P-factor to a high AOA [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]], so the forces are not constant. Allowing the airplane to yaw is a listed climb error [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and yaw at the stall is what starts a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The ACS power floor is 65 percent (AI.X.D.S4).

questions.q: In a clean power-on stall at full power, your learner notices the break came below the bottom of the green arc and decides the airspeed indicator must be faulty. What do you explain?
options: The indicator is faulty: installation error is greatest at high power settings, so any stall that breaks below the green arc means a pitot or static problem to write up
Same critical AOA: the arc marks a power-off stall speed, and power lowers the stall speed, as in the PHAK sample table (clean, wings level: 54 knots power on, 65 off)
The nose was much higher, so the wing reached a higher AOA than in a power-off stall, and a higher stalling AOA always gives a lower stalling airspeed with the power on
The airplane was lighter than the arc assumes, and weight is the only factor that moves the stall below the green arc, since power does not change the stall speed at all
questions.why: A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, whatever its airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. VS1, the bottom of the green arc, is usually the power-off stall speed at maximum takeoff weight, clean [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. In the PHAK sample table, gear and flaps up, wings level, the stall is 54 knots power on and 65 knots power off [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Airspeed indicator errors are generally greatest at low airspeeds, not at high power [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. Weight does move the stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]], but it is not the only factor, so the 'weight only' answer fails too.

questions.q: For a power-on accelerated stall your learner levels at the briefed VA for today's weight, leaves climb power in and rolls into a coordinated 45° bank. As he starts the pull, the airspeed is climbing past VA. What do you teach?
options: Pull harder and sooner, because a firmer pull bleeds off the extra speed quickly, and the VA limit applies to the roll-in, not to the pull that follows it
Carry on, because the VA limit in the ACS applies only to the power-off version, and the power-on version stalls at a lower indicated airspeed anyway
Stop the pull, reduce power and let the speed settle at or below VA before adding back pressure, so the wing stalls before it can be overstressed
Extend partial flaps to slow down, because flaps add drag and also lower the stall speed, which keeps the break well below VA during the steep turn
questions.why: The ACS asks for power set so the airspeed does not exceed VA or any other POH/AFM limit (AI.X.E.S4), and the AFH says never above the manufacturer's speed, VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. At or below VA the wing reaches the critical AOA, which unloads it, before the design load limit; above VA it can reach the limit load first, so more pull can overstress the airplane [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. A harder pull above VA is exactly that case. The load factor at the stall equals the square of the speed ratio [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], so the faster the airplane, the more G the wing can make before it stalls. Flaps are never used for accelerated stalls because the design G limits are lower with them out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: In the 45° turn of an accelerated stall setup, the nose falls below the horizon and the airspeed starts to build toward VA. Your learner pulls back on the yoke without changing the bank, and the turn tightens. What do you teach?
options: Good: more back pressure raises the nose and the lift, so he should keep pulling until the warning comes, which is the point of the Task
Add power so the climb brings the nose up, because power holds the altitude in a bank, and the bank itself can stay where it is
Shallow the bank first, then raise the nose: pulling with the bank unchanged tightens the turn and can lead to a diving spiral
Push the yoke forward and keep the 45° bank until the airspeed falls back, because the turn can only tighten once the wing has stalled
questions.why: AC 61-67C says that if the nose falls during a steep turn, the pilot might raise it without shallowing the bank, and this tightens the turn and can lead to a diving spiral [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The speed then builds, and above VA the airplane can be overstressed before it stalls [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; the ACS asks for power set so the speed does not exceed VA (AI.X.E.S4). The fix is to shallow the bank first, then raise the nose. Power does not cure it, and a push with the bank held keeps the airplane diving and the speed rising.

questions.q: One lesson flight with a CFI applicant: power-off stalls, then the cross-controlled stall demonstration, then spins. The highest terrain in the practice area is 1,850 feet MSL. Under the CFI ACS, what is the lowest MSL altitude at which each Task may be completed?
options: 3350 feet for all three, because the AFH 1,500-foot AGL recovery floor applies to every stall and to every intentional spin
4850 feet for all three, because any stall flown on a lesson that also includes spins takes the 3,000-foot floor of the spin Task
3350 feet for the power-off stalls, 4850 feet for the cross-controlled stall and 5350 feet for the spins
3350 feet for the power-off stalls, 4850 feet for the cross-controlled stall and 5850 feet for the spins
questions.why: Each Task has its own S2 floor: power-off stalls no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (AI.X.C.S2), the cross-controlled stall no lower than 3,000 feet AGL (AI.X.F.S2) and spins no lower than 4,000 feet AGL (AI.X.I.S2). With terrain at 1,850 feet: 1,850 + 1,500 = 3,350; 1,850 + 3,000 = 4,850; 1,850 + 4,000 = 5,850 feet MSL. These are completion floors, so each entry must be higher by the airplane's own altitude loss. The AFH 1,500-foot AGL figures [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] and AC 61-67C's 'above 3,500 feet AGL' for spin training [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]] (which gives 5,350) are not the checkride numbers, and spins carry 4,000 feet, not 3,000.

questions.q: On base, you see another airplane already established on final ahead of you. Your learner, who is lower, says she has the right of way and tightens the turn to final to get in front of it. What do you teach?
options: Right of way settles it: the lower airplane goes first, so a steeper bank and a little inside rudder to line up fast are acceptable
The right of way does not allow cutting in or overtaking; if the turn would create a hazard or is being rushed, abandon the approach and go around
Speed up on base and take a steep bank to beat the other airplane to the runway, because extra airspeed gives the margin for a tight turn
Tighten the turn with a 45° bank but no rudder, since the AFH accepts a steep bank near the ground when traffic is close and only a skid is a problem
questions.why: The airplane at the lower altitude has the right of way, but pilots should not use that rule to cut in front of or overtake an airplane on final; if the turn would create a collision hazard, a go-around or avoidance maneuver is in order. A pilot trying to overtake may be tempted to make an overly steep turn, and rushing the turn is a good reason to abandon the approach and go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. That rushed turn is the start of the cross-controlled stall: low in the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30° and do not skid, because the airplane may rapidly enter a spin; the safest action is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: On a go-around from a hazy night approach, your learner adds full power and feels a strong sense that the nose is far up. With no clear horizon he pushes the nose well below the climb attitude. What do you teach?
options: Trust the feeling: the seat knows the nose is too high, so he should hold the lower nose until the sense of a high nose is gone
Pull the power back to idle for a moment, because a quick deceleration cancels the false feeling and lets him see the true attitude
Look down and trim nose-down until the feeling stops, because trim is the fastest way to remove the sensation without moving the controls
Expect that false nose-up feeling from the rapid acceleration; hold the climb attitude on the attitude indicator, not by feel
questions.why: A rapid acceleration, such as full power, can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, especially with poor visual references, and the disoriented pilot may push the airplane nose-low [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Spatial disorientation from these illusions can be prevented only by reference to reliable fixed points or to the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. A quick power reduction has the opposite effect, and the pilot may pull the nose up toward a stall [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Looking down at the trim wheel is a head movement that can set off the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. The AFH go-around needs forward pressure and right rudder to hold a safe climb attitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; set that attitude on the instruments.

questions.q: Practicing go-arounds at altitude from a full-flap glide, your learner's callout is 'Flaps up, pitch up, power.' On the next one he raises all the flaps, pitches up, the airplane settles and the horn sounds before the power is in. What order do you teach, and why?
options: Power, attitude, configuration: full power smoothly first, then forward pressure and right rudder for a safe attitude, then the flaps up in small increments
Pitch, power, flaps: set the attitude first so the airspeed is protected, then add full power, then raise all the flaps at once so the drag goes away as quickly as possible
Flaps, power, pitch: drag is the main enemy at low speed, so raising the flaps first is right, and his only mistake was pitching up for the climb before the power was in
Power, flaps, attitude: full power first, then all the flaps up at once to stop any ballooning, and only then raise the nose, since the trim will hold it during the cleanup
questions.why: The AFH gives three cardinal principles in order: power, attitude, configuration. Full or maximum allowable power goes in smoothly and without hesitation; the pilot resists any pitch-up while the airspeed is insufficient, expects considerable forward pressure and uses right rudder; and the flaps come up in small increments, because a sudden, complete retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. AC 61-67C shows the secondary stall link: retracting the flaps rapidly while holding a higher than normal climb pitch can give a secondary stall or settling with altitude loss [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Improper pitch attitude is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: In the secondary stall demonstration you recover from a full-flap, gear-down, power-off stall. The learner adds power and climbs with the flaps still full out, at what looks like a normal climb pitch, and the horn comes back. What do you tell him?
options: A secondary stall needs an abrupt pull, so the horn is a fault, and he can hold the same pitch while the speed builds
Pull the nose up higher so the airplane climbs through it, because the full flaps give extra lift and the horn only means that the climb is getting steep
In some airplanes even a normal climb pitch with flaps out gives a second stall; lower the nose until the horn stops, then flaps up in small steps
Raise all the flaps at once to clear the horn, because the drag is the problem, and then hold the same pitch as the airplane accelerates
questions.why: AC 61-67C's go-around exercise: after a full-flap, gear-extended, power-off stall, recover and try to climb with the flaps extended. A higher than normal climb pitch gives a secondary stall, and in some airplanes a stall occurs even at a normal climb pitch. Retracting the flaps rapidly while holding a higher than normal pitch can give a secondary stall or settling with a loss of altitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. A secondary stall may follow any recovery that does not reduce the AOA enough [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], and it is recovered like any stall: nose down until the warning is gone [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Then the flaps come up in small increments as the airplane accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: In your own secondary stall demonstration you let the ball slide to the right during the abrupt pull. At the second break the right wing drops and the nose yaws right. What is the recovery, and what is the lesson?
options: Reduce the AOA until the warning stops, cancel the yaw with rudder, level the wings, then add power; the lesson is to keep the ball centered through the pull and the recovery
Level the wings with aileron first, then lower the nose, because the dropped wing is the urgent problem and the stall clears once the wings are level
Add full power and hold the nose attitude, because the thrust stops the yaw and the wing drop, and the lesson is to start every demonstration with the power up
Push the nose far down and hold it until the airspeed is well into the green arc, because the yaw does not matter once the nose is low
questions.why: Recovery is the generic template: reduce the AOA until the stall warning is gone, roll the wings level, and proactively cancel yaw with rudder so the stall does not progress into a spin; power is added as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. A secondary stall is recovered the same way [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Aileron before the AOA is reduced can deepen the stall at the wing tip [[24:120|AFH 5-15]], and power alone does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. A spin needs a stall plus yaw at or beyond the stall, and a pilot who caused the yaw with rudder may not know the critical AOA is exceeded until the airplane yaws toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

questions.q: A learner asks you to show him a spin in a normal category trainer with the placard 'No acrobatic maneuvers including spins approved.' A fellow CFI says the placard is only a technicality because the airplane passed spin testing. What do you say?
options: He is right if you stop at one turn, because one turn is what the certification testing covered, and the placard no longer applies below that limit

Decline: with that placard intentional spins are not authorized, and there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin, because normal category testing covered only a one-turn or 3-second spin
He is right, because any airplane that passed spin testing can be spun with a CFI aboard when the weight and CG are inside the limits
Decline only if there are no parachutes, because the placard is waived once each occupant wears an approved parachute and a CFI gives the instruction
questions.why: If the manufacturer does not specifically approve an airplane for spins, intentional spins are not authorized by the CFRs or suggested by the AFH; the official sources are the TCDS, the AFM/POH limitations and a placard. In an airplane placarded against spins there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin, and some instructors wrongly call the restriction a technicality. Normal category certification required recovery only from a one-turn or 3-second spin in no more than one additional turn [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Behavior beyond that is unknown, which is the reason for the placard [[13:21|AC 61-67C 400a]], and the pilot should assume the airplane may become uncontrollable in a spin [[13:22|AC 61-67C 402]]. A parachute does not change the placard.

questions.q: Your applicant recovers cleanly from a spin to the left. As the rotation stops she suddenly feels as if the airplane is spinning to the right, and she starts to press left rudder against that feeling. What do you tell her?
options: A new spin to the right has started: add full left rudder and brisk forward elevator, as in the first recovery, and hold them until it stops
It is a graveyard spiral: she should pull back firmly to stop the loss of altitude and then level the wings once the sense of turning is gone

It is the graveyard spin illusion: the inner ear gives a false spin the other way, so trust the instruments and the rising airspeed, neutralize the rudder and ease out of the dive, or she may spin left again
It is the coriolis illusion from her head movement: she should hold the rudder against the feeling until it goes away and keep her head still
questions.why: A proper recovery from a spin that has stopped stimulating the inner ear can create the illusion of spinning the other way, and the disoriented pilot will return the airplane to the original spin: the graveyard spin [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Such illusions are prevented only by reference to reliable fixed points or the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Rising airspeed shows the airplane is no longer in a spin; the rudder is neutralized once rotation stops, because holding it causes yaw or sideslip, and back pressure is applied gently, since too much can cause a secondary stall and another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The graveyard spiral is a different illusion, felt in a coordinated constant-rate turn, that makes a pilot pull back, and the coriolis illusion comes from a sharp head movement [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]].

questions.q: The evaluator, playing your learner, enters a spin with full rudder but lets the elevator come only halfway back. The nose drops steeply and the airspeed rises through 100 knots and keeps climbing. Which error do you name, and which recovery fits?
options: A fully developed spin with a fast rotation: power to idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, then brisk forward elevator held until the airspeed stops rising
Recovery rudder that was not brisk enough: hold full opposite rudder longer and pull firmly, because the rising airspeed shows the wing is no longer stalled
An accelerated spin caused by power: leave the rudder in, close the throttle and wait, because a trainer recovers on its own within half a turn once the power is off
Not holding full up-elevator on entry, giving a spiral, not a spin: idle, unload to about 1 G, roll level with coordinated controls, then raise the nose gently
questions.why: 'Failure to apply and maintain full up-elevator pressure during spin entry, resulting in a spiral' is the second AFH spin error, and its spiral recovery is: power to idle, some forward elevator to unload to about +1G, roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then gently raise the nose and climb only once the speed is safe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. If the airspeed is increasing, the airplane is no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]; AC 61-67C also tells you to recognize the spiral by rapidly increasing airspeed and recover at once [[13:20|AC 61-67C 300f]]. Spin recovery inputs treat a stall that is no longer there, and pulling back rapidly while rolling level is the reaction the AFH says can create loads that damage the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: Your applicant learned on power-off stalls never to pick up a dropping wing with aileron before the AOA is reduced. In her first spin recovery she neutralizes the ailerons, then, as the rotation slows, adds aileron against the rotation 'to help level the wings sooner'. What do you teach?
options: Good technique: aileron against the rotation works like extra opposite rudder and shortens the recovery, as long as the forward elevator is already in
Keep the ailerons neutral: aileron against the spin can flatten it and may even make it unrecoverable, and aileron with the spin can speed the rotation
Use aileron with the rotation instead, because that lowers the AOA on the descending wing and so stops the autorotation sooner than the rudder alone
The ailerons do not matter in a spin, because the whole wing is stalled and they have no effect at all; only the rudder and elevator change the recovery
questions.why: Step 2 of the AFH spin recovery is ailerons neutral: aileron in the direction of the spin may speed the rotation, steepen the attitude and delay the recovery, and aileron opposite the spin may flatten the spin, delay the recovery or even cause an unrecoverable spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. AC 61-67C also has the pilot neutralize the ailerons [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]], and the manufacturer's procedure comes first [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Her stall habit points the same way: aileron used before the AOA is reduced can deepen the stall at the tip [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The ailerons are not without effect; that is why the AFH warns about them.
